text: An automated (or autonomous) guided vehicle that moves materials along predefined routes using guidance built into the facility, such as magnetic tape or buried wire, and stops when its path is blocked.
A safe point directly above (or in front of) a pick or place position, usually computed as an offset from the grip point, where the robot slows down before the final straight-line move.
The self-driving system on NASA's Perseverance rover that maps the terrain in 3D, finds hazards and plans a path around them while the rover is moving.
In ISO 8373, a machine's ability to perform intended tasks based on its current state and sensing, without human intervention; it comes in degrees rather than being simply on or off.
The maximum permissible physical force (in Newtons) and pressure (in N/cm²) that a human body zone can absorb without sustaining pain or injury.

A functional safety networking design where safety and standard communication integrate on one transmission medium by treating the underlying network as unreliable and placing diagnostics entirely in end devices.
Letting the robot round a corner near a programmed point without stopping, set with ABB zonedata such as z50 or a URScript blend radius r; a fine or r=0 point stops exactly.
A fast, compiled programming language that is the other main ROS language and the basis of Arduino sketches, used when code must run quickly and close to the hardware.
A program that reads and reports the state of a robot cell (robot mode, safety status, I/O, sensor checks) without controlling it or clearing stops.
A functional safety protocol enabling standard and safety devices to operate together on the same network using time-stamped data and production identifiers.
A collaborative robot designed to work alongside people in a shared space, with speed and force limits configured as part of its setup.
The formal standard term designating that safety is a characteristic of the complete robotic task, tooling, and environment, rather than the arm alone.
Counts Per Revolution; the total number of decoded state transitions (up to 4x PPR) registered by the control system per full shaft revolution.
Data Distribution Service, the industry-standard middleware that ROS 2 uses by default to let nodes discover each other and exchange messages without a central master.
How ROS 2 nodes find each other on a network: DDS participants announce themselves with discovery messages, so the local network and firewall must let those messages through.
A formal declaration that a contributor created the submitted code or has the right to share it under the project's open-source license, confirmed by adding a Signed-off-by line to commits.
A virtual 3D simulation of a physical robot, cell, and environment used to test, program, and debug operations without stopping the real production line.
A safety control function designed to avert or reduce emerging hazards by stopping dangerous motion, classified under ISO 13850 as Category 0 or Category 1.
A manually operated, three-position control switch that permits robotic motion only when maintained in its intermediate position, stopping motion if released or gripped tightly.
An industrial Ethernet technology where slave devices with dedicated EtherCAT Slave Controllers read and insert data on the fly as standard frames with EtherType 0x88A4 pass downstream.
A move ending in which the robot reaches the programmed point and stops before continuing (fine in RAPID, blend radius r=0 in URScript), used where the gripper opens or closes.
A fail-safe device in PROFIsafe; implementing the PROFIsafe protocol alone cannot turn a standard device into one, because its safety level depends on its safety hardware architecture.
A formal test of a completed robot cell at the builder's shop before shipment. It checks build quality, wiring, safety interlocks, and basic operation to find problems early.
An issue label that explicitly marks issues that are easier than normal and reserved exclusively for newcomers who have never contributed to open source before.
Diodes or a similar path placed across a motor or its driver so that the current of an inductive load has somewhere safe to go when it is switched off, protecting the driver from voltage spikes.
The standard ROS action (control_msgs) for sending a robot arm a timed list of joint positions, with feedback during the motion and an error code at the end.
The core six ethical obligations established by the NSPE Code of Ethics, led by the paramount duty to protect public safety, health, and welfare.
A vendor-neutral software standard from EMVA that provides a universal programming interface and feature naming convention for industrial machine vision cameras.
Virtual spatial boundaries enforced by software or safety controllers to restrict where a robot or its tool can travel, preventing it from leaving designated safe working zones.
A system design where a human must actively approve each action before the robot executes it, such as a surgeon confirming a cut proposed by a surgical robot.
Sequential Function Chart, a graphical programming language defined in IEC 61131-3 for industrial PLCs that organizes machine operations into steps, transitions, and action blocks.
The Layer 2 timing and synchronization standard in Time-Sensitive Networking, based on IEEE 1588, that gives all devices on an Ethernet network a shared clock.

The IEEE's code for its members, last revised in 2020, which includes holding public safety paramount, protecting others' privacy, treating people fairly and not retaliating against people who report violations.
Modbus exception code 02 indicating that the register address received in the request is not allowed for the server.
A robot arm used in manufacturing, such as a six-axis welding arm, that follows precisely programmed paths and must be repeatable, safe and predictable.
A switch on a guard or door that stops the machine when the guard is opened, with coded types that are harder to defeat.
The international standard for industrial robot safety, with Part 1 covering robots and Part 2 covering robot applications and cells, both revised in 2025.
The international standard that defines robotics terms. Its 2021 edition defines a robot as a programmed, powered machine with some autonomy to move, handle objects, or position tools.
The standard for the mechanical interface of a robot's tool flange, where a code like 50-4-M6 means a 50 mm pitch circle with four M6 screws.
An older dual H-bridge motor driver board that controls two DC motors. Because its internal transistors drop substantial voltage, it produces noticeable heat and needs a large heatsink.
The triangle rule c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos C, used in two-link inverse kinematics to find the elbow angle from the distance to the target.
A managed ROS 2 node that moves through explicit states—Unconfigured, Inactive, Active, and Finalized—so a robot system can start up, configure hardware, and shut down safely.
The procedure (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147) of switching off and locking a machine's energy sources and tagging them so nobody can restart it during servicing.
The principle in robotics ethics and international law requiring human supervision, situational awareness, and the ability to intervene or deactivate autonomous weapons before lethal force is used.
A socio-technical dynamic where a human operator bears legal and moral responsibility for a system failure despite having limited control over automated behavior.
The standard autonomous navigation system for ROS 2, enabling mobile robots to map environments, avoid obstacles, and follow global paths.
The National Society of Professional Engineers' code of conduct for engineers, which opens with six Fundamental Canons headed by holding paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public.
An open industrial communication architecture (IEC 62541) that lets plant machines and IT systems exchange structured data securely across different platforms using TCP port 4840.
An ISO 13849-1 rating from PL a to PL e of how reliably a safety function, such as stopping when a door opens, does its job.
How tightly a robot's attained positions cluster when it is sent to the same pose many times, the precision figure quoted on most datasheets (ISO 9283).
A collaborative safety method in which contact with a person is allowed but the robot's design or safety functions keep force and pressure below set limits.
A functional safety communication standard under IEC 61784-3-3 complying with SIL 3 under IEC 61508 and PL e category 4 under ISO 13849.
A controller-initiated stop caused by proximity to a limit where the robot halts program execution while retaining electrical power.
Quality of Service: ROS 2 settings such as reliability, history depth and durability that a publisher and subscription choose for a topic, and that must be compatible for them to connect.

How much a messaging system guarantees about delivery. MQTT has three levels (at most once, at least once, exactly once); ROS 2 uses QoS policies such as reliability and durability (see Quality of Service (QoS)).
A set of communication rules in ROS 2 that controls how messages are delivered, including reliability, history depth, and whether past messages are saved for new subscribers.
An ABB motion control feature that shortens cycle times by automatically calculating the highest safe acceleration and deceleration for the robot at every moment.
A robot system together with its safeguarding, the machines it works with and the protected space around it, set up to do one production job.
A standard ROS node that reads joint angles and the robot's URDF model to compute and broadcast Cartesian 3D coordinate transforms via tf2.
In ISO 8373, a mechanism built with robotic technology that does not meet every part of the robot definition, such as a teleoperated remote manipulator with no autonomy.
A software bridge that translates standard ROS messages, topics, and services into the specific network commands required by a robot manufacturer's proprietary controller.
An open-source initiative and industry consortium that brings ROS and ROS 2 software libraries, standard interfaces, and drivers to factory automation and industrial robot arms.
The standard 3D graphical visualization tool in ROS that renders sensor streams, coordinate frames, point clouds, and robot URDF models from live topic data.
The validated, password-protected robot controller settings (safety planes, speed and force limits, stop functions, safeguard I/O) that no program or AI tool should change.
A robot controller board whose diagnostic LEDs show normal communication with a slow green flash and hardware or safety errors with permanent red.
The minimum distance between a protective device such as a light curtain and the hazard, set so the machine stops before a person can reach it.
The use of robots to look for survivors in places too dangerous or tight for rescuers, first tested at scale in the rubble of the World Trade Center in 2001.
A numbered list of the steps a cell performs, each with the condition that must be true before the step can start.
Slowing a planned trajectory in time to match how fast the robot is actually allowed to move, for example when the pendant speed slider is lowered or the controller slows the arm for safety.
Semantic Robot Description Format: a file used by MoveIt alongside the URDF that names planning groups and poses and lists link pairs that never need collision checks.
The current a DC motor draws when its shaft is held still with full voltage applied, usually the highest current it will ever draw.
A multiplier (such as 1.5 for smooth parts or 2.0 for porous ones) applied to the calculated holding force so a suction cup holds firmly during fast robot movements.
A risk assessment that lists every task people do at a robot cell, such as clearing jams or teaching, and scores the hazards of each task separately.
The ISO 12100 order for reducing machine risk: first design the hazard out, then add guards and protective devices, then give warnings and training for what remains.
A set of IEEE 802 Ethernet standards that provides guaranteed bounded latency, synchronized clocks, and low packet loss for real-time industrial and control traffic.
A ROS 2 Quality of Service setting where the publisher saves past messages so newly connected subscribers receive the latest data immediately, useful for static maps.
The practice of simulating and testing robot trajectories, PLC logic, and safety interlocks in a 3D virtual cell before physical machinery is built.
An independent hardware or software timing circuit that triggers a safe stop state if the main controller fails to send a periodic refresh signal.
What turns a robot arm into a working cell: components, safeguarding and light-curtain distance, PLC-robot handshakes, integrator roles with FAT and SAT, three typical cells, cycle time and cost.

Build a complete pick-and-place cycle in URSim (and RobotStudio): TCP and payload, a three-point fixture frame, approach offsets, exact stops at the grip, and re-teaching only three points when the fixture moves.
How ROS 2 drives real industrial arms: ROS-Industrial, the common driver pattern, and the UR, ABB, FANUC, KUKA and Yaskawa drivers, with real-time and safety limits.

A practical integrator workflow for robot cell safety: the ISO 12100 three-step method, task-based risk assessment, guards and safety distances, performance levels, robot safety functions and lockout/tagout.
Electrical and I/O troubleshooting: multimeter voltage and continuity checks, discrete sensor wiring, 24 V power budgets, and fieldbus diagnostics.

Capstone project: build a simulated pick-and-place work cell in URSim or ABB RobotStudio with gripper I/O, a safety configuration and a FAT-style test sheet, graded by milestones and a four-level rubric.
Capstone project: build an Arduino speed-controlled wheel with a quadrature encoder, H-bridge driver, PID loop and a state machine with ramps and a FAULT state, with milestones, safety and a rubric.
